extracted.intended_audience: architects, art historians, and students of Venetian architectural history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, dating, and evaluating Venetian architectural features (bases, doorways, jambs, capitals) by close formal and executional analysis; emphasizes physical examination of mouldings and comparative morphology as evidence. Useful for attributing works to Byzantine, Gothic, or later schools and for assessing quality/authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of contemporary sources over restored history
rubrics_metrics.description: The only history worth reading is that written at the time of which it treats; one fresh draught of such history is worth more than a thousand volumes of abstracts, reasonings, and suppositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer first-hand, contemporaneous documents and direct observations as superior evidence to later restorations or secondary syntheses when judging buildings or historical events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dating by careful personal examination of mouldings and features
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements respecting dates of Venetian buildings are founded on careful and personal examination of all the mouldings or other features available as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect multiple examples of evidence-bearing details (bases, doorways, capitals, tracery) and illustrate representative exceptional forms; a subset of well-chosen examples can suffice to prove a dating claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity and simplicity of Byzantine bases as dating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity and simplicity of the Byzantine bases in general, and distinctions between Torcello, Murano, and St. Mark's bases, tend to prove earlier dates attributed to island churches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare base forms across sites: close resemblance to Murano or Torcello forms argues for earlier (Byzantine) dating; compile plate comparisons to show relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slurring of the upper roll into the cavetto indicates early relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: The slurring of the upper roll into the cavetto (seen in certain figures) establishes relationship between important buildings and is strong presumptive evidence of early, rather than late, period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the upper roll flows into the cavetto (rather than being sharply separated), treat this as a signal of earlier workmanship and use it to link and date buildings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incision between upper roll and cavetto and sloping ledge diagnostic of Byzantine form
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine bases, if they have an incision between the upper roll and cavetto, are apt to approach a form where the upper roll is cut out of the flat block and the ledge beneath is sloping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the presence of an incision and sloping ledge beneath the roll (compare specific numbered examples) as a Byzantine/early trait distinct from later Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper roll proportion as chronological indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: If the upper roll is larger than the lower (exceptional form), this is never the case in late Gothic, where the proportion is always as in the late Gothic figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the relative sizes of upper vs lower rolls on bases: an upper roll at least as large as the lower suggests earlier dating; the reverse proportion indicates later Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fillet profile (sloping vs vertical) as dating clue
rubrics_metrics.description: The sloping fillet between upper roll and cavetto is common down to late periods; the vertical fillet is found in Byzantine ones. A sloping fillet is strong presumptive evidence of belonging to an earlier period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe whether the fillet is sloping or vertical—sloping often signals earlier work; vertical fillet tends to align with Byzantine examples depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steep profile as a notable diagnostic feature
rubrics_metrics.description: A peculiarly steep profile (e.g., No. 22) is a characteristic point to note with reference to its implications for date and type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark unusually steep profiles as significant and compare with documented examples and prior appendix notes to refine dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Door type (ogee porch with square-headed real entrance) as descriptive taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrances to St. Mark's consist of great circular or ogee porches underneath which the real open entrances are square-headed; the jamb mouldings of these doors are highly curious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify doors by porch form vs inner opening: the combination (ogee outer, square-headed inner) helps place doors in a typological and chronological framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary, hand-drawn carving indicates free Byzantine workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: The carvings and incisions on certain jambs are arbitrary, evidently drawn by hand (none being segments of circles, none like another), indicating the free work of the time; often poor in effect but characteristically free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret irregular, non-geometric carving as evidence of Byzantine-era workmanship and of craftsmen working by eye rather than systematic moulding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finials, complete ogee arch, and abandonment of lintel indicate late school
rubrics_metrics.description: Some doors are shown to be of a late school by their finials; the latest school is indicated by a complete ogee arch (instead of round or pointed) and the abandonment of the lintel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the presence of elaborate finials, full ogee arches, and lack of a lintel as markers of the later architectural schools and later chronological phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square doors akin to St. Mark's as evidence of early/original structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the city we find doors resembling the square doors of St. Mark, occurring with rare exceptions in Byzantine period buildings or embedded in restored houses; never forming a connected portion of late buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a building contains square-headed doors of this type as original elements, consider that building as belonging to the earliest period of the Gothic school or as retaining Byzantine features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradation of ornament toward arch apex indicates Gothic sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: In some doors each square ornament (each containing a rose) diminishes to the apex of the arch—an interesting and characteristic circumstance showing the subtle feeling of Gothic builders—they diminish ornamentation to sympathize with the delicacy of the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for systematic diminution of ornament toward the arch apex as a Gothic design principle signalling refinement and sensitivity to overall form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences of level and systematic projection in Byzantine jambs
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal points in Byzantine mouldings are curious differences of level (delineated by dotted lines) and the systematic projection of the outer or lower mouldings in many examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stepped levels and outward projection of lower mouldings as distinctive Byzantine traits and as dating evidence when comparing jamb profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of jamb profile into archivolt/traceries indicates Gothic development
rubrics_metrics.description: In Gothic jambs some profiles are continuous into the archivolt and meet the traceries, with semicircular or half-shaft elements sustaining traceries—features scarcely represented in Venetian Byzantine forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify jambs that flow into archivolts/traceries as Gothic characteristics; the presence of continuous shafts/pier forms supports dating to the Gothic period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitals cut for their specific place as evidence of Venetian workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain capitals were cut for their place in the apse (one side turned to light, the other to shade), providing conclusive proof that these capitals were cut for their place and therefore are tests of Venetian workmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitals that are carved specifically for their installed orientation as strong indicators of local (Venetian) cutting and authenticity; such fitting argues for original workmanship rather than later reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular, non-correspondent foliage as hallmark of Byzantine designers
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine designers display irregular and fearless freedom in foliage—no two parts correspond; foliage carved without symmetry is characteristic and picturesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat asymmetric and irregular foliage carving as a diagnostic sign of Byzantine-era design and a hallmark of earlier Venetian carving traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four principal orders of Venetian capitals and floral correspondences
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four principal orders of Venetian capitals (two great concave and convex groups, and two transitional) with examples related to flower-forms (lily, Tulipa sylvestris, magnolia) which help to typify forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capital profiles and their floral analogues as typological markers; identifying which 'order' (concave/convex/transitional) a capital belongs to aids in stylistic classification and dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convex/convexity associated with earliest dating and heaviness
rubrics_metrics.description: The convex forms are heaviest and are the earliest in date; convex forms are positioned lower in the plate because of their weight and early chronology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regard convex capital profiles as earlier types relative to concave or later-developed profiles when building a relative chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressive development from truncated capitals to enriched Gothic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest truncated capital (rounded to fit the shaft) developed into capitals with a leaf beneath each truncation, leaves curling into a spiral, then the addition of shields or roses—the formed capital of the early Gothic and later richer rose capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace capital evolution in a building: simple truncation → angle leaves with spirals → added ornament (shield/rose) → rose capitals; each step provides relative dating information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rose capitals and ball-flower evolution as chronological markers
rubrics_metrics.description: The rose in capitals, initially flat and quatrefoiled, becomes a round ball dividing into three leaves (resembling English ball-flower) and later a projecting bud; the transition indicates relative lateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the morphological state of the rose/ball-flower motif—flat quatrefoil → three-leaf ball → projecting bud—as an indicator of later development in the Gothic sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of four shorter leaves as an important early thirteenth-century innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of four other shorter leaves at the sides (to the existing three/angle leaves) was taken early in the thirteenth century and became the basis for the best Venetian capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a capital shows the expanded leaf arrangement (angle leaves plus four side leaves), treat it as characteristic of the important thirteenth-century Venetian development and often a mark of high quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of Corinthian volute and Lombardic Gothic leaf forms as influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaves used in later Venetian capitals lost the Corinthian volute and became pure plain leaves of the Lombardic Gothic of the early thirteenth century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the loss of classical volute forms and the adoption of Lombardic pure leaf shapes as indicators of Lombardic Gothic influence and appropriate dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution technique (incised leaf with raised rib vs bold projecting leaf) as dating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: In early capitals a leaf at the angle is cut into the stone in the manner of an Egyptian bas-relief with a raised edge and a raised rib up the centre; in later, more elaborate capitals the leaf is thrown out boldly with an even edge and enriched on its own surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between intaglio-style execution (cut-in leaves with raised ribs) indicating early date and high precision, versus applied, projecting, richly-carved leaves indicating later elaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late Gothic exaggeration and corruption as negative quality marker
rubrics_metrics.description: Late Gothic capitals (e.g., fig. 15) are generally characteristic of the late fourteenth and early fifteenth century and notable for their exaggeration and corruption; certain monuments (like St. Mark's screen, dated 1380) demonstrate the entire corruption of Gothic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat excessive delicacy, over-elaboration, and stylistic corruption as signs of late, degenerate Gothic work rather than high-quality earlier Gothic; use dated benchmarks (like the screen) to set terminus ante quem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of magnification to read small diagnostic details
rubrics_metrics.description: A magnifying glass will disclose small but diagnostic details (e.g., diminution of ornaments toward the arch apex; Bondumieri and Leze shields on keystones; fine ridges and ribs on capitals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ close visual aids to observe tiny features that carry evidence for dating, authorship, or stylistic attribution; do not rely solely on distant inspection.
